flawed_step: The assertion that local Hamiltonicity forces a global Hamiltonian cycle is false.
counterexample: Let G have vertices 1,...,11. Begin with the triangular bipyramid on {1,2,3,4,5}: triangle 123, with 4 and 5 each adjacent to 1,2,3 but not to each other. Insert vertices 6,7,8,9,10,11 into faces 412,423,431,512,523,531 respectively, joining each inserted vertex to all three vertices of its face. Thus N(6)={4,1,2}, N(7)={4,2,3}, N(8)={4,3,1}, N(9)={5,1,2}, N(10)={5,2,3}, and N(11)={5,3,1}. This face-stacking construction is a maximal planar graph. Explicit Hamiltonian cycles in the neighborhoods of vertices 1 through 5 are respectively (4,6,2,9,5,11,3,8), (4,7,3,10,5,9,1,6), (4,8,1,11,5,10,2,7), (1,6,2,7,3,8), and (1,9,2,10,3,11). For vertices 6 through 11, each neighborhood is its defining triangle. Hence G is locally Hamiltonian. However, {6,7,8,9,10,11} is an independent set of size 6, while only five other vertices exist. A cycle cannot contain two consecutive vertices from this independent set, so an 11-vertex Hamiltonian cycle could contain at most five of them. Therefore G has no Hamiltonian cycle.
assessment_summary: The explicit 11-vertex stacked triangulation is locally Hamiltonian but non-Hamiltonian, refuting the universal claim.
